articles.title: Illegal immigrant tuition perks put 4 states in Trump DOJ crosshairs
articles.summary: Arizona State University gave 432 illegal immigrants in-state tuition in Fall 2025, totaling $10.5 million in reduced costs, the Justice Department alleges.
articles.body: The Trump administration filed lawsuits against four states Thursday over laws allowing illegal immigrants to receive financial benefits offered to state residents, including in-state tuition, state grants and state-funded student loans. The Justice Department argued that laws in Oregon, Washington, New Mexico and Arizona allowing illegal immigrants to receive benefits are in violation of a federal law that states an illegal immigrant is ineligible to receive higher education in-state benefits unless those same benefits are available to every U.S. student. "This is a simple matter of federal law: Colleges cannot provide benefits to illegal aliens that they do not provide to U.S. citizens," Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate of the Justice Department’s Civil Division said in a statement. "This Department of Justice will not tolerate American students being treated like second-class citizens in their own country." DOJ SUES NEW JERSEY OVER LAWS GIVING ILLEGAL ALIENS IN-STATE TUITION, SAYS CITIZENS TREATED AS 'SECOND-CLASS' The latest lawsuits bring the number of states facing legal challenges over laws granting illegal immigrant students the same benefits as lawful residents to 21. The Justice Department has won its cases in Texas, Kentucky, Oklahoma, Nebraska and Illinois. "Our efforts will not cease until President Trump’s promise is fulfilled: Illegal aliens will not receive benefits denied to American citizens," Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward, Jr. said in a statement. The difference between in-state and out-of-state tuition costs at public universities in the four states is significant. The complaint showed that for the 2026-2027 school year, Washington residents would pay $13,406, compared with $44,460 for out-of-state students at the University of Washington. This means illegal immigrants could receive a $31,054 discount if they earned a high school diploma or equivalent in the state, lived there for at least one year for reasons other than attending college and signed an affidavit saying they would seek permanent residency when eligible. TRUMP'S JUSTICE DEPARTMENT SUES NEW YORK, OTHER BLUE STATES OVER TUITION FOR ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS The Justice Department's lawsuit against Arizona also showed a significant difference between in-state and out-of-state tuition costs, with the largest gap at Arizona State University totaling $24,448. The lawsuit alleged that in fall 2025, 432 illegal immigrants received in-state tuition benefits at Arizona State University amounting to $10.5 million in reduced tuition. The lawsuit also cites a report from the Arizona Center for Investigative Reporting that estimates more than 3,600 illegal aliens per year could qualify for in-state tuition under Arizona’s law. A spokesperson for the Arizona Board of Regents, a plaintiff in the lawsuit, said the school system follows state law. "We are reviewing the lawsuit and will work closely with Arizona leaders on the appropriate next steps," a spokesperson said. The benefits extend beyond tuition costs. COURT CHECKS PRITZKER AS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION SCORES ANOTHER IMMIGRATION WIN In Oregon, only in-state students enrolled at Oregon Health & Science University can receive a Rural Nurse Scholars Scholarship, which covers the full cost of tuition and a $1,500 travel stipend. The Justice Department alleges that illegal immigrants are eligible for the scholarship under state law. In Washington, not only do illegal immigrants qualify for in-state tuition and grants, but the state also created a financial aid program for illegal immigrants living in the state who are unable to obtain federal financial aid. The program is known as the Undocumented Student Support Loan Program, and it was created under a bill passed in 2020. Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson said in a statement to Fox News Digital that he stands by the state's laws. "Washington state won’t be bullied into changing how we provide opportunities for young people in our state," Ferguson said. "We’ll see them in court, and we expect to win." A June 2024 report estimated that roughly 408,000 illegal immigrants were enrolled in higher education, with 29.1% arriving in the United States at age 17 or older. articles.title: Ohio family decries use of photo in Republican Senate ad
articles.summary: Republicans are facing backlash for a Senate campaign ad that tied Democratic candidate and former Sen. Sherrod Brown (Ohio) to a highway accident. The victims’ family is speaking out against the use of their story in the political ad. Brown’s race against incumbent Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) is one of the most competitive contests in…
articles.body:
Republicans are facing backlash for a Senate campaign ad that tied Democratic candidate and former Sen. Sherrod Brown (Ohio) to a highway accident. The victims’ family is speaking out against the use of their story in the political ad.

Brown’s race against incumbent Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) is one of the most competitive contests in the tense battle to win the Senate majority.

The National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC), which fundraises for and supports Senate Republican candidates, paid for a short ad, mostly on streaming services and devices, that ties Brown’s stance on immigration to a fatal traffic crash involving two young parents and their 1-year-old son.

“Brown opened our border to dangerous illegals,” a voiceover says in the ad, before briefly describing the accident and showing a picture of the Soposki family, all of whom died after a semitruck crashed into their car.

The driver of the semitruck was Modou Ngom, an immigrant who came to the United States in the 1990s and was naturalized as a citizen in 2015. Ngom is now under investigation by Immigration and Customs Enforcement for allegedly using fraudulent names and dates of birth to obtain an ID.

The ad highlights a key dynamic in the fight for the Senate, as Republicans look to make immigration a central issue. Republicans in Congress and President Trump have repeatedly tied illegal border crossings and crimes committed by immigrants to Democratic policies around the country.

But the Soposkis’ relatives did not approve of the use of their family’s story in the Ohio ad. Jesse Mallen, whose sister Lynnea died in the crash, wrote to the Husted campaign privately and asked it to take down the ad, according to The New York Times .

The ad has stopped running after more than two weeks, although a clip of it remains on the NRSC’s YouTube page . Husted, speaking to Spectrum News on Thursday, clarified that the ad was not from his campaign but from “some third-party group.” At the end of the ad, a line notes that it was authorized by Husted’s campaign.

When asked if it would be taken down, he said “of course.”

“If a family was victimized by an illegal alien who killed a family member, I don’t want them to have to suffer anymore,” Husted said. “So I hope they’d take it down, which I understand they did.”

The NRSC, in a statement, repeated the sentiment of the ad.

“For 32 years, radical leftist Sherrod Brown backed open border policies that cost Ohioans their lives, without ever apologizing,” said Nick Puglia, a spokesperson for the NRSC. “Our ad campaigns will continue to hold Sherrod Brown accountable.”

articles.title: Accused WWII Memorial vandal: ‘I made a big mess to get the nation’s attention’
articles.summary: The woman accused of vandalizing the World War II Memorial on the National Mall earlier this month said during a new interview that she did it to “get the nation’s attention.” Melissa Farris, 41, told The Washington Post she graffitied the memorial in an attempt to spotlight what she alleges was wrongdoing by a former…
articles.body:
The woman accused of vandalizing the World War II Memorial on the National Mall earlier this month said during a new interview that she did it to “get the nation’s attention.”

Melissa Farris, 41, told The Washington Post she graffitied the memorial in an attempt to spotlight what she alleges was wrongdoing by a former union employer in Kentucky.

“Veterans fought for people, not monuments or memorials, and I honor veterans by trying to keep our liberties and life and happiness here,” she said in the interview, which was published Thursday. “One thing everybody can agree on is everybody loves to hate on something.”

“So, I made a big mess to get the nation’s attention,” she added.

Farris was arrested two weeks ago after prosecutors say she livestreamed herself writing “Clean hands Dirty $” in orange spray paint on the inside of the memorial’s Atlantic Theatre Pavilion and poured dish soap into the fountain.

A federal grand jury on Thursday indicted Farris on one count of destruction of veterans’ memorials and one count of destruction of federal property. Each felony charge carries a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison.

“I believe now that I was extremely naïve,” she told the Post. “I thought Washington is where you go to practice democracy. It broke my heart to walk into our nation’s capital. I think that I idealized it.”

Farris was released from jail a few days after her arrest but was ordered to surrender her passport and stay away from the memorial. A D.C. magistrate judge also barred her from traveling outside of the northern Ohio and eastern Michigan area, where she lives.

Federal prosecutors had urged the judge to keep her behind bars, raising concerns in court filings that the woman’s “history and characteristics” indicate she may be a flight risk.

“Defendant was defiant and outspoken before, during, and immediately after committing her crimes,” U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro wrote in an Aug. 17 motion. “Her attitude only changed after she did not receive the attention she so desperately craved, demonstrating that any expressed remorse is insincere.”

Farris is set to appear before U.S. District Judge Trevor McFadden in D.C. for a hearing on Thursday.

The stunt successfully grabbed President Trump’s attention, who wrote in a Truth Social post a few days before Farris’s arrest that authorities were homing in on people suspected of damaging the site.

“Our beautiful World War II Memorial was just hit by Spray Painting Vandals,” he wrote. “THERE CAN BE NO GREATER INSULT TO THOSE AMERICAN HEROES IN WORLD WAR II. First the Reflecting Pool, now this. We are on their trail! Where do these animals come from???”

The Post reported that Farris received dozens of angry messages on social media after the incident, and that she and her family had also gotten death threats. But the 41-year-old appeared unfazed by the criticism.

“I can unite a nation quicker than anybody else, apparently, because it didn’t matter what political party they were,” she told the newspaper. “They can still all hate me, and then I’m going to give them the truth.”

articles.title: Milo Yiannopoulos held in ICE custody
articles.summary: Far-right political commentator Milo Yiannopoulos was taken into custody by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and is being held at a detention center, according to the agency’s online detainee database. The British native served as chief of staff for the rapper Ye, formerly Kanye West, and was in Louisiana ahead of Ye’s scheduled concert…
articles.body:
Far-right political commentator Milo Yiannopoulos was taken into custody by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and is being held at a detention center, according to the agency’s online detainee database.

The British native served as chief of staff for the rapper Ye, formerly Kanye West, and was in Louisiana ahead of Ye’s scheduled concert in New Orleans on Friday night, according to TMZ, which first reported his detainment.

According to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), Yiannopoulos was apprehended Thursday night at the Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport (MSY) in Kenner, Louisiana.

DHS stated “Yiannopoulos legally entered the country on May 14, 2019, through New York City, New York. He chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws.”

“Yiannopoulos was issued a final order of removal by an Immigration Judge on July 22, after failing to show up for his immigration hearing,” DHS continued in their statement. “He will remain in ICE custody pending removal.”

Far-right influencer Laura Loomer, who had a public fallout with Yiannopoulos, is taking credit for first sharing news of his immigration status.

Loomer alleged in December that Yiannopoulos overstayed his visa and has been illegally residing in the U.S., including staying at the homes of former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene (R-Ga.) and podcaster Candace Owens.

In a social media post, Loomer claimed Yiannopoulos called for her to be “assassinated” at the height of their feud, prompting her to report his immigration status to authorities.

“When Milo called for me to be assassinated, I reported him to ICE and the FBI,” she wrote on the social platform X .

Yiannapolous is known for his close ties to Ye and served as his director of political operations during Ye’s 2024 presidential campaign. The British commentator has also been a public supporter of ICE operations and has previously called for “total legal immunity” for ICE agents while performing their duties.

“California needs ICE checkpoints at supermarket entrances, gas stations, strip malls, intersections and government buildings, with on the spot deportation for anyone who can’t prove they are in the US illegally,” he wrote social media in June 2025 .

articles.title: Tempe mayor on move to cancel Flock cameras: ‘Potential for misuse was too great’
articles.summary: Corey Woods (D), the mayor of Tempe, Ariz., on Thursday defended his decision to cancel the city police department’s $80,000 contract with Flock Safety, a top automated license plate reader company, amid reported misuse of its products. “The concern that we had was just that the potential for misuse was too great,” he told NewsNation’s…
articles.body:
Corey Woods (D), the mayor of Tempe, Ariz., on Thursday defended his decision to cancel the city police department’s $80,000 contract with Flock Safety, a top automated license plate reader company, amid reported misuse of its products.

“The concern that we had was just that the potential for misuse was too great,” he told NewsNation’s Blake Burman.

“In order to make sure that we’re not only just being directly upfront with our residents, our main goal was to provide public safety, but also make sure that we’re protecting public trust,” Woods continued. “And we understood that the longer this kept going on, we were going to see an erosion in public trust from the people who live, work and play in the city of Tempe.”

While Woods noted the city had not discovered any instances of Tempe law enforcement officers misusing Flock camera data, the mayor pointed to concerning reports from police departments across the country.

Earlier this month, The Washington Post uncovered 50 instances in which police officers were accused of abusing Flock’s network of roadside cameras to spy on people. One officer in Georgia searched his ex-girlfriend’s plates in Flock’s system more than 500 times.

Woods said his decision to turn off these roadside cameras, which went into effect Wednesday morning, was supported by an “overwhelming majority” of Tempe residents.

“But I did get a smattering of other folks who reached out and said, ‘Hey, I think these were good tools for law enforcement, and I wish you could have just come up with some safeguards to have protected residents’ privacy as opposed to doing away with the entire system,’” he added.

The company has added several privacy guardrails in the wake of growing backlash, including reducing the default video retention period from 30 days to seven days, adding more detection measures for suspicious searches and providing greater transparency about their products.

A Flock spokesperson told The Hill in a statement Friday that the company respects the city’s decision to cancel the contracts.

“Flock has built the most accountable tool in police technology, and our technology gives communities control over how their systems are used, including the ability to adopt shorter data retention periods, strong access and auditing policies, and safeguards specifically designed to catch potential misuse,” the spokesperson said. “We believe Tempe could have preserved the system’s value in helping solve serious crimes while still respecting privacy, and taking that tool away does not make a community safer.”

The reported misuse of Flock’s sprawling roadside network has prompted calls for company accountability from Capitol Hill lawmakers.

Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.), who chairs the Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism, launched an investigation this week into accusations that the company “assembled an unprecedented national surveillance network” of more than 120,000 cameras across 49 states.

The senator demanded that Flock CEO Garrett Langley explain the safeguards the company uses to protect citizens’ data.

“Congress never authorized the network your industry has built,” Hawley wrote in his letter to Langley on Wednesday. “Your company’s internal policies are, in practice, the only safeguards for hundreds of millions of Americans. People across the country are now discovering that fact and demanding answers from their elected officials.”

articles.title: Jeffries, Ocasio-Cortez look to November at 2026 March on Washington: ‘The tide is coming’
articles.summary: Civil rights leaders and Democratic lawmakers, alongside hundreds of protesters, rallied on the National Mall on Friday to commemorate the 1963 March on Washington, with many speakers emphasizing the importance of November’s midterm elections. The 2026 “Defend the Vote” March on Washington, organized by the Rev. Al Sharpton’s National Action Network and Martin Luther King…
articles.body:
Civil rights leaders and Democratic lawmakers, alongside hundreds of protesters, rallied on the National Mall on Friday to commemorate the 1963 March on Washington, with many speakers emphasizing the importance of November’s midterm elections.

The 2026 “Defend the Vote” March on Washington , organized by the Rev. Al Sharpton’s National Action Network and Martin Luther King III, took place 63 years after the iconic march where Martin Luther King Jr. gave his famous “I Have a Dream” speech.

The speakers at this year’s march included House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger (D), Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin and National Urban League President Marc Morial.

Many of the speeches focused on Democrats turning out to vote in November for the midterms, while decrying recent Supreme Court decisions on voting rights and the Trump administration’s actions that speakers condemned as having negative effects on Black Americans.

Jeffries used his speech at Friday’s rally to implore attendees to get out the vote in November.

“We certainly have come a long way in the United States of America, but we still have a long way to go,” Jeffries declared.

“These are challenging times in this country right now. We have a hater in the White House, a reckless and costly war of choice raging in the Middle East, a Supreme Court that’s out of control,” he said, before arguing that Black Americans are particularly hard hit by the Trump administration’s policies.

Jeffries concluded his brief remarks by urging Americans to vote for Democrats in order to take back the House in November so that the nation can “continue our march towards a more perfect union.”

“This November, the first of many tides is coming,” she told attendees, urging them to “summon the collective genius” of the 1963 march.

“The tide is coming, and this time we intend to win it all,” she said.

While introducing Ocasio-Cortez, Sharpton notably compared her to the late New York Rep. Shirley Chisholm, who ran a groundbreaking campaign for the Democratic presidential nomination in 1972. The comparison comes amid speculation about Ocasio-Cortez’s potential presidential candidacy in 2028.

Spanberger told the attendees about her state’s progress and urged them to continue the fight against the Trump administration at the ballot box this November.

“The right to vote is about more than a ballot, it’s about whether we believe every person should have a voice in our democracy,” Spanberger stated, listing off a number of progressive milestones the Old Dominion had made since she took office and noting “all of that happened because of voting.”

Spanberger concluded her remarks by declaring, “Let’s vote this November and let’s win!”

Morial told the assembled crowd that “you cannot say ‘America First’ while you suppress the vote,” referencing President Trump’s campaign slogan.

“We say it’s time to put the American people first,” he added before listing several progressive agenda items he said would be on the ballot in November.

“We will fight until hell freezes over, and then we’ll fight on the ice,” said Morial, who noted that he’s participated in the numerous commemorations of the 1963 march.

Sanders struck a slightly different tone than many of the other speakers, stressing that Martin Luther King Jr. believed “political freedom and economic freedom are inseparable” and that “it’s not only voting rights that are under assault today.”

Sanders emphasized that the 1963 march was the “March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom” and reminisced about how he attended the event as a college student, calling it an experience that he has never forgotten and one that has had a lasting impact on his life.

“Tragically, that dream of a more just and equitable society has never been under greater threat than it is right now,” Sanders said, referencing Martin Luther King Jr.’s “I Have a Dream” speech.

articles.body: The woman accused of vandalizing the World War II Memorial in Washington, D.C., was formally indicted Friday, Fox News Digital has learned. Melissa Farris was charged on two counts, including destruction of a veterans’ memorial and destruction of government property. The Kentucky woman allegedly spray-painted the words "Clean hands, dirty money" in bright pink paint and dumped bubble soap into the fountain at the center of the memorial, according to authorities. WORLD WAR II MEMORIAL ON NATIONAL MALL VANDALIZED WITH PINK SPRAY; FOUNTAIN OVERFLOWING WITH BUBBLES Federal prosecutors allege that cleanup and restoration costs already exceeded $1,000. Farris did a Facebook live before turning herself in and her arrest Aug. 14, in which she admitted to the alleged vandalism the day before. "It's me. I am going to turn myself in," she said. "I'm outside district federal court. I am just trying to do the right thing. … I was trying to get people to listen. … I tried to reach the media. I tried to fight back. I tried to ignore it." Farris claimed she lived in a paper-thin camper that she "boarded up with cardboard in the winter to feel a little bit warmer." Fox News Digital has reached out to the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia for comment. WWII MEMORIAL VANDALISM SUSPECT IN CUSTODY, CHARGED WITH TWO FELONIES, PIRRO SAYS "Vandalizing our World War II Memorial is a despicable attack on a sacred monument honoring the Americans who fought and died for our freedom," U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro said in a statement after Farris was charged. articles.title: Massie urges passage of PRIME Act following Trump move to ease meat processing restrictions
articles.summary: GOP Rep. Thomas Massie (Ky.) reupped his calls Friday for Congress to remove barriers for local meat processors after President Trump announced he would make it easier for ranchers to process their own food. “This is great, but it should be a law, not just an executive order,” Massie wrote in a social media post,…
articles.body:
GOP Rep. Thomas Massie (Ky.) reupped his calls Friday for Congress to remove barriers for local meat processors after President Trump announced he would make it easier for ranchers to process their own food.

“This is great, but it should be a law, not just an executive order,” Massie wrote in a social media post , referring to his proposed Processing Revival and Intrastate Meat Exemption (PRIME) Act.

The legislation would allow local slaughterhouses to sell meat in state without being subject to federal inspection requirements. The bill has “dozens of bipartisan sponsors” in both chambers of Congress, the lawmaker said.

Massie first unveiled a version of the PRIME Act in 2015 and introduced it again as recently as July 2025.

A pilot version of the proposed act was included in the House farm bill, which passed the lower chamber in April. However, the program is not included in the Senate’s version of the legislation package, which is still under consideration in the Senate Agriculture Committee.

“Pass the PRIME Act so consumers can get affordable U.S. beef and farmers can flourish!” Massie added Friday.

The president’s decision to ease meat processing restrictions followed backlash from Republicans and ranchers surrounding his administration’s plans to temporarily lift higher tariffs from imported ground beef products.

The move would allow up to 300,000 metric tons of ground beef to be imported without “out-of-quota” tariffs within a 90-day period and then sold within the U.S. at 25 percent below market prices, Trump said last week. Critics have argued this would unfairly penalize U.S. ranchers and farmers.

The president defended his move, saying it would allow the U.S. cattle population to replenish and bring down rising costs for consumers. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins told reporters earlier this week the details of the plan are still under discussion.

In a Friday Truth Social post announcing these changes, Trump emphasized, “Ranchers and Farmers have always been a number one priority for me.”

“They work very hard, are smart, efficient, and immaculately CLEAN, but for years I have heard that they have had a tremendous problem with the Big Processors, who many say are a nasty Monopoly,” he wrote.

The president said he was “authorizing legal documents” to allow farmers and ranchers to process their own meat, saying this change “should move quickly.”

The National Cattlemen’s Beef Association (NCBA), which lobbies on behalf of large meatpacking conglomerates, criticized Trump’s latest move in a Friday statement shared on social media.

“NCBA supports more competition, more opportunities for small & regional processors, and eliminating unnecessary regulations but weakening federal meat inspection & food safety standards isn’t the answer,” the organization said.

“America’s cattle producers have earned consumer trust in U.S. beef over generations,” its statement continued. “That trust, and the gold standard food safety system behind it, shouldn’t be put at risk for a short-term political fix.”

articles.title: Elon Musk enters the midterm chat: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, we dive into Elon Musk’s first foray into this year’s midterms. Plus, Kristen Welker digs into how voters are feeling about the Iran war six months in. Sign up to receive this newsletter in your inbox every weekday here. Elon Musk enters the midterm chat By Andrew Arenge and Ben Kamisar Elon Musk is back. The tech billionaire’s super PAC launched digital ads this month in three states with key Senate races: Maine, Michigan and New Hampshire. The effort from America PAC targets specific lists of people and urges viewers to register to vote, according to a review of Meta political ad data. Some ads are generic, featuring reminders that the Senate races in their states could decide control of the chamber. Others go on the attack against socialism, including one ad that features an image of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, warning that “if you don’t vote in November, socialism could declare victory over America.” The campaign marks America PAC’s first significant ad spending since the April 2025 Wisconsin Supreme Court election. Musk injected himself into the center of that race, spending millions of dollars and traveling to the state. But his endorsed candidate, conservative Brad Schimel, ultimately fell well short of Susan Crawford, allowing liberals to maintain their majority on the swing state court. Musk spent a quarter-billion dollars to boost Trump and the GOP in the 2024 election. He then went on to serve as an adviser to Trump at the outset of his second term, before having an on-again, off-again relationship with the president after leaving the White House. It remains to be seen exactly how much Musk will spend this time around. But as the Republicans prepare to face a daunting political environment this fall, any financial involvement from Musk in battleground contests will be a welcome development for the party. Read more → Voter frustrations with Trump and the GOP reshape the midterm map Analysis by Kristen Welker As the war with Iran hits the six-month mark, Americans appear to have reached a consensus: They don’t support it. That was the case when the war started, and it remains so in recent polling over the last few weeks. Poll after poll shows that President Donald Trump’s handling of the war is deeply underwater and that voters are skeptical it will come to an end any time soon. It’s a reminder of the political headwinds Trump and Republicans face across multiple fronts. In addition to this conflict, Trump continues to escalate trade wars with countries like Canada, while capturing headlines for trying to rename Lake Ontario or threatening to demolish the Kennedy Center. We’ve spoken with voters across the country who keep making the same point — they’re laser-focused on the economy and frustrated about the war, with many worried the administration’s efforts aren’t hitting the mark. Those frustrations are one reason why even traditionally red states like Texas — the home of one of my guests this Sunday, Republican Sen. Ted Cruz — appears to be in play this cycle. Democratic state Rep. James Talarico is waging a tough battle there against state Attorney General Ken Paxton in what’s become a major proving ground for so many of these issues. Most recently, Talarico has blasted Trump’s effort to suspend tariffs on beef exports as part of a broader attempt to hit the GOP on the issue of rising costs. But that issue in particular has scrambled the usual party lines: A chorus of Republican lawmakers around the country has also warned the plan could hurt American farmers and ranchers. Paxton, meanwhile, has countered with an affordability pitch of his own centered on lowering taxes, as he and Trump try to frame Talarico as too extreme on social issues. In a sign of how competitive the race has become, Trump also traveled to the state for a fundraiser yesterday. Cruz and Rep. James Clyburn, D-S.C., will join me on “Meet the Press” this Sunday to discuss all of this and more. That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.

"First of all, they’re showing a White House staffer who is staffing the White House, but ultimately, they are trying to make this false story of Natalie Harp having some illicit affair with Trump come true -- and pretend that Harp would be so embarrassed by it that she would actually ‘still show her face’ in the Oval Office," Young continued. articles.title: Crockett suggests she won’t campaign with Talarico, will focus ‘down ballot’
articles.summary: Rep. Jasmine Crockett (D-Texas) said she will focus on “campaigning down ballot” in Texas, suggesting that she won’t campaign with Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico after he defeated her in the party’s primary. “We’ve seen the turnout that you can produce. Talarico might very well need that magnetism. Will you campaign with him?” CNN’s Laura…
articles.body:
Rep. Jasmine Crockett (D-Texas) said she will focus on “campaigning down ballot” in Texas, suggesting that she won’t campaign with Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico after he defeated her in the party’s primary.

“We’ve seen the turnout that you can produce. Talarico might very well need that magnetism. Will you campaign with him?” CNN’s Laura Coates asked the congresswoman on Thursday.

“I will be campaigning down ballot,” Crockett said.

“Because when we’re looking at a state like Texas, we’ve tried this, where we’ve got one amazing candidate that’s running at the top of the ticket,” Crockett said, when asked why she drew the distinction.

She pointed to Democrat Beto O’Rourke, who came within a few points of ousting Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) in 2018, as an example of a top-of-ticket candidate who was “raising all the money, doing all the things, running around the entire state, but it’s not enough.”

“And so for me, I think that making sure that people that maybe are getting overshadowed because it seems like it’s only about one big race, I think amplifying them, making sure that I can raise their profiles and introducing them to people, that’ll give something more to voters.”

Crockett, whose last-minute decision to enter the race for Sen. John Cornyn’s (R-Texas) seat roiled the Texas political landscape, lost the Democratic primary to Talarico this spring. The popular congresswoman, known for her viral moments in the House, pledged to support his bid — but she’s since kept her distance from Talarico’s campaign.

In May, she announced plans to launch a leadership PAC to help other candidates, called FIRE, which stands for Fuel Individual Rights Everywhere. All five Texas candidates backed by her PAC won their primary runoffs later that month.

Among them was a proxy win over Talarico: former Rep. Colin Allred (D-Texas), endorsed by Crockett , won the Democratic nod for a Dallas-area House seat over Rep. Julie Johnson (D-Texas), who was supported by Talarico .

The wins were a signal of Crockett’s political strength after her loss to Talarico assured her House tenure will end in January.

Meanwhile, Talarico faces Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) in a toss-up race. Republicans have long dominated the Lone Star State, but Democrats are optimistic that Talarico could notch the party’s first statewide win in decades.

Decision Desk HQ considers the race a toss-up, but it forecasts that Talarico is narrowly favored to win over Paxton, whose bid has been dogged by scandal .

Pressed by CNN’s Laura Coates on whether it’s an “either-or” choice between campaigning for the top of the ticket or down the ballot, Crockett said that for her, “it probably is.” She said she’s being pulled all across her “really big state” with FIRE PAC , and there are candidates she “didn’t get to do anything for” while running her Senate race.

articles.title: Trump administration asks Supreme Court to allow military’s transgender ban
articles.summary: The Trump administration is asking the Supreme Court to allow the Pentagon to enforce a ban on transgender troops serving in the military, rocketing the issue up to the high court for a second time. The petition asks the justices to weigh whether the ban is constitutional and reverse an appeals court decision that blocked…
articles.body:
The Trump administration is asking the Supreme Court to allow the Pentagon to enforce a ban on transgender troops serving in the military, rocketing the issue up to the high court for a second time.

The petition asks the justices to weigh whether the ban is constitutional and reverse an appeals court decision that blocked the administration from using it to expel members who are already serving.

Solicitor General D. John Sauer argued the block was a “gravely erroneous holding,” writing the authority of the U.S. military to determine who can serve in the armed forces is a “matter of exceptional importance.”

“Whether the Constitution prohibits the military from exercising that authority by adopting a policy like the one here is a recurring issue, which has arisen before and will likely arise again absent this Court’s review,” he wrote.

The justices have sole discretion over which cases they take up and will likely consider the petition during a closed-door meeting when they return from summer recess.

President Trump issued an executive order shortly after returning to the White House that banned all transgender troops from the U.S. military, arguing they threaten readiness and undermine unit cohesion.

The decision was criticized by a group of Senate Democrats, arguing the commander in chief was violating the service members’ civil rights and hindering U.S. national security.

In the months since, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has signed various documents to carry out the directive. Hegseth signed a memo in February last year that transgender service members would be removed within 60 days unless they were granted a waiver showing their support of “warfighting capabilities.”

Many transgender service members have voluntarily left the military since.

Hegseth has railed against transgender people in recent weeks, using a slur during his speech at the Iowa State Fair earlier this month when speaking about transgender troops in the military.

During a speech this week in Oshkosh, Wis., the Defense secretary said the Pentagon is focused on restoring “warrior ethos,” which means “no more DEI [diversity, equity and inclusion].” He continued, “It means colorblind, gender neutral, merit-based, back to basics across the board no matter if you’re carrying a rifle or you’re working on the plant floor.”

A divided panel for the U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia found in June that the policy was motivated by animus against transgender people and violated their constitutional right to equal protection.

“The sharp contrast to the Mattis Policy, adopted in the first Trump Administration, which allowed servicemembers who were transgender or who had suffered from gender dysphoria to remain in the military, appears to be driven by the bare desire to harm a politically unpopular group: persons who identify as transgender,” U.S. Circuit Judge Robert Wilkins wrote in the appeals court decision .

The 2-1 ruling barred the Pentagon from enforcing the ban against a group of active service members who had brought the challenge. It did not, however, extend that to people seeking to enlist in the U.S. military.

U.S. Circuit Judge Justin Walker, a Trump appointee, reminded his colleagues that “we are judges not generals” in a dissenting opinion.

Lawyers representing the plaintiffs urged the Supreme Court on Friday to reject the administration’s request, noting the case is scheduled to go to trial in January.

“The Trump administration wants the Supreme Court to rush in and bless the expulsion of proven, decorated soldiers before a single court has issued a final judgment,” Shannon Minter, the legal director for the National Center for LGBTQ Rights, said in a statement . “There is no circuit split, no emergency, and no merit – only a policy that multiple courts have now found was driven by prejudice rather than military need.”

The Supreme Court allowed the administration to temporarily move forward with the policy in a ruling on the emergency docket in May 2025, lifting a nationwide injunction in a separate case. The court’s three liberal justices dissented.

That lawsuit, which was brought in February on behalf of seven openly transgender service members, another transgender person who wishes to enlist and an advocacy group, is pending at the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals.

articles.body:
Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee (R) announced a proposal Friday to rename Nashville’s airport in honor of Dolly Parton, following the late country music star’s death earlier this week.

“Dolly Parton’s extraordinary life is forever woven into the fabric of our state,” Lee said in a statement announcing the proposed change.

“From her rural mountain home in East Tennessee to global stages, Dolly carried the Volunteer Spirit with her,” the governor continued. “At a place where Tennessee welcomes the world, it is fitting that Nashville International Airport would bear the name of our state’s favorite daughter and greet travelers with the enduring legacy of Dolly’s music, generosity, faith, and kindness.”

The legendary singer was raised in a one-room cabin in Sevier County, Tenn., as the fourth of 12 children. Parton remained heavily invested in the state after her rise to fame, sponsoring college scholarships for Tennessee students and holding a benefit concert to raise money for a new hospital in the county.

The country music star died in Nashville at 80 years old Tuesday.

The Metropolitan Nashville Airport Authority (MNAA) will discuss renaming Nashville International Airport at a meeting Sept. 17, according to the airport’s Friday press release .

MNAA President and CEO Doug Kreulen celebrated Parton’s “remarkable legacy” in a statement.

“She understood that dignity, kindness and opportunity should never be defined by where you come from or your socioeconomic status. At BNA [Nashville International Airport], we share that commitment,” Kreulen wrote.

“Whether you are boarding a private aircraft or taking your first flight, you deserve to be welcomed, respected and served with the same level of care,” he continued. “That spirit is what defines BNA and it is a fitting reflection of the values Dolly shared with Tennessee and the world.”

Many state and national leaders from across the aisle honored the late singer’s legacy after the news of her death earlier this week, including former presidents .

On Thursday, Maine Gov. Janet Mills (D) shared a photo on social media of the governor’s residence “lit pink in honor of Dolly Parton.”

“Her extraordinary talents as a singer and songwriter will never be forgotten, nor will her lifelong commitment to giving back to her community and helping others,” Mills wrote. “Maine will always love you, Dolly!”

GOP Rep. Diana Harshbarger, who represents the area of Tennessee where Parton was raised, said the state has “lost one of our own.”

“When you say the iconic name Dolly, everyone in east Tennessee knows who you’re speaking about,” the lawmaker told CNN’s Phil Mattingly on Tuesday. “And it’s a sad day because she never forgot where she came from and she never forgot where her roots are, and that’s right here in the 1st District of Tennessee in Sevier County.”

articles.title: Trump administration appeals latest temporary block on mail-in voting changes
articles.summary: The Department of Justice (DOJ) on Friday appealed a temporary block on the U.S. Postal Service’s new mail-in ballot regulations, an apparent bid to fast-track legal proceedings as the midterms loom just months away. The notice from DOJ lawyers follows a late-night ruling from a federal judge in Boston on Thursday that barred the Trump…
articles.body:
The Department of Justice (DOJ) on Friday appealed a temporary block on the U.S. Postal Service’s new mail-in ballot regulations, an apparent bid to fast-track legal proceedings as the midterms loom just months away.

The notice from DOJ lawyers follows a late-night ruling from a federal judge in Boston on Thursday that barred the Trump administration from implementing certain provisions of the Postal Service’s rule for at least 14 days.

U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani sided with a group of Democratic-led states and private rights groups that have been fighting President Trump’s executive order in court, finding that they were likely to succeed in their claims that the restrictions are unconstitutional.

She also contended that it would be “practically impossible” for states to fully comply with the rule by November given the tight timeline, posing an “overwhelming risk” of disenfranchisement for voters who rely on mail ballots.

“In light of the State election officials’ unrebutted declarations that compliance with the Final Rule at this late date is impossible, the risk of irreparable harm to voters in those jurisdictions is grave,” said Talwani, an appointee of former President Obama.

The jump to the 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals caps off what has been an up-and-down week in the Trump administration’s effort to crack down on mail-in voting during a pivotal election cycle.

The Postal Service issued its final rule last Friday and had said as recently as Thursday that it was in effect, coming on the heels of a procedural victory at the Supreme Court at the start of the week.

The high court, over the dissent of the three liberal justices, held that a previous challenge from blue states had been brought prematurely so Talwani lacked authority to block it.

The justices did not weigh whether the rule was ultimately lawful, saying only that parties had to wait until it was finalized to sue.

That prompted Talwani to lift her remaining nationwide injunction despite finding that the administration had violated her earlier order by moving ahead with the rule.

Challengers argued in new filings this week that the restrictions interfere with the states’ constitutional authority to administer their own elections, asking the court to block the requirements again now that they believe they have standing.

The Justice Department pushed back on the notion that the federal government was trying to seize control of elections, writing that the rule imposed only “modest informational requirements.”

“The Rule does not displace a single State election law. And it need not and should not prevent a single voter from voting by mail,” DOJ lawyers told the court.

articles.title: Jelly Roll explains political beliefs after Trump roasts: I’m ‘down the middle’
articles.summary: Country music star Jelly Roll defended his political beliefs during his final hosting appearance on “Jimmy Kimmel Live!” Thursday night, responding to widespread criticism from President Trump supporters. “Just because I watched a fight on TV doesn’t mean I support everything this administration does,” Jelly Roll said in his opening monologue, referring to the White…
articles.body:
Country music star Jelly Roll defended his political beliefs during his final hosting appearance on “Jimmy Kimmel Live!” Thursday night, responding to widespread criticism from President Trump supporters.

“Just because I watched a fight on TV doesn’t mean I support everything this administration does,” Jelly Roll said in his opening monologue, referring to the White House’s UFC Freedom 250 event . “Just like hosting Jimmy Kimmel’s show doesn’t mean I have all of Jimmy’s politics.”

“Sure, I lean left on some things, but like most folks, I’m pretty down the middle. I am a Christian. I am a country music singer. I’m a farmer. I’m a bow hunter,” he continued.

Jelly Roll, whose real name is Jason DeFord, made jokes throughout the week about Trump, causing many of his supporters to label the artist a “traitor.”

Since his music career has taken off, Jelly Roll admitted he’s strayed away from making political statements. But the singer has been an advocate for fentanyl awareness in the U.S. and testified on Capitol Hill last year in favor of legislation combatting the fentanyl crisis.

“These people [drug users] crave reassurance that their elected officials actually care more about human life than they do about ideology and partisanship,” he said in his speech on Capitol Hill, thrusting himself into the political spotlight.

The rapper-turned-country singer, who recently lost about 300 pounds, poked fun at Trump’s weight on Monday. Jelly Roll compared his weight loss to “an entire Donald Trump,” and said “let’s be honest, based on his approval ratings, it seems like most of the country wants to do the same thing.”

“From one fat pig to another, take it from me that physical fitness is very important. Trust me, you’ll be happy to see your penis again,” he continued.

Trump supporters weren’t the only ones to gang up on the country star, as GOP Rep. Jimmy Patronis (Fla.) said Jelly Roll was no longer welcome in his Florida Panhandle district.

“I don’t even want to see his bus on I-10,” Patronis wrote Wednesday on the social platform X . “He’s always been the token ‘country’ star the libs in California are allowed to enjoy (He ain’t country, never was.).”

Patronis went on to say the singer suffered from “Trump Derangement Syndrome.”

Jelly Roll initially responded to Patronis and Trump supporters Tuesday night, joking that he never thought he would get in more trouble than Rosie O’Donnell — who consistently feuds with Trump.

But the artist’s Thursday night monologue expanded beyond his political wisecracks from earlier in the week, adopting a more serious tone and discussing his beliefs.

The country music star said that, while he is normally quiet about his political affiliation, he now believes it’s time to make a change.

“I spent my entire career trying not to belong to a political party. Partly because until March of this year, I wasn’t even allowed to vote,” he said, in reference to his now-pardoned felony conviction. “But now that I have that right, it’s one I plan to exercise this coming November.”

He was pardoned by Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee (R) in December 2025 after he was convicted of a 2005 robbery, possession with intent to sell cocaine and breaking parole. He was released from prison in 2016.

“I’m going to try and do the right thing right now because human dignity isn’t Republican nor Democrat,” Jelly Roll continued, appearing to choke up while addressing Kimmel viewers.

Near the conclusion of his monologue, the artist took one last jab at both Republicans and Democrats, saying that “our leaders on both sides of the aisle are doing an absolute s‑‑‑ job of trying to bring us together.”

articles.title: LGBTQ group reveals which Dem nominee is sponsoring Halloween event featuring drag shows
articles.summary: Keisha Lance Bottoms is sponsoring a Halloween event featuring drag shows, and her record on gender policy and the Riley Gaines Act faces scrutiny.
articles.body: As the Trump administration’s efforts have choked off federal funding for LGBTQ groups, Keisha Lance Bottoms, former mayor of Atlanta and Georgia's Democratic gubernatorial nominee, is sponsoring an upcoming Halloween event open to children that will include drag shows. "From 5-8, the little monsters roam free trick-or-treating through spooky trails and glowing Halloween worlds, and when night falls, the hallo queen show explodes with music, costumes and pure Halloween spectacle," ColGay Pride, an LGBTQ+ group based in Columbus, Georgia, said in a video. Notably, the group’s programming states that the "adults-only" portion of the night, which includes the drag shows, will begin after 9 p.m. Even so, Lance Bottoms’ support of the Halloween event, which includes a haunted walk, s’mores, an adult-and-kids costume contest — all centered around gender expression — adds to her record of supporting LGBTQ-related content around children. POWERFUL LGBTQ+ GROUP'S ENDORSEMENTS COULD TANK VULNERABLE DEMS OVER RADICAL YOUTH TRANS AGENDA ColGay Pride describes its goal as "promoting diversity, inclusion and equality for the LGBTQ community in Columbus and the surrounding areas and create a supportive and affirming environment through our programs and events." The group, which is throwing its final Halloween celebration after 13 years, said President Donald Trump’s federal funding cuts had made it dependent on individual contributions. "We are closing our doors next year," the group wrote. "It has become far too difficult to raise money when our financial aid was cut off completely under Trump, when our own citizens — the very people we have served for twenty years — do not donate. Sometimes you simply reach a point where enough is enough." The group thanked Lance Bottoms for her support in a post to Facebook with a "digital sponsorship certificate." It’s unclear how much she contributed to the event. Bottoms' gubernatorial bid has been complicated by political liabilities. The Campaign Finance Commission fined her $37,000 in 2021 for accepting over $60,000 in contributions that exceeded legal limits and $110,000 that exceeded debt caps. She also announced that she would not pursue re-election as mayor of Atlanta amid a COVID-19 crime during which homicides spiked by 58% over levels from the year before. In addition to those controversies, Bottoms has received criticism from conservatives for her stances on gender policy. GOP FRONTRUNNER IN KEY GUBERNATORIAL RACE FORCED TO ANSWER ABOUT HIRING ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS: 'I DON'T KNOW' Recently, in a gubernatorial debate, the former mayor said she would have vetoed the Riley Gaines Act, a piece of legislation that banned biological men from competing in women’s sports. "I believe that decisions about who competes and how people compete shouldn’t be happening at the state Capitol. I don’t support the government making decisions about who should compete in athletics. I believe that decision should be left to respective athletic associations," Bottoms said. That comment, in particular, has become a key campaign quote for her opponent, Rick Jackson, a businessman and the Republican nominee to replace outgoing Gov. Brian Kemp, as they set out to attack Bottoms' far-left positions on issues of gender and sexuality. "Keisha Bottoms and the other Democrats said they’d have vetoed the Riley Gaines Act. They won’t protect girls’ sports, but they will open the floodgates for woke ideology in our schools. We’re going to make sure they don’t get the chance," the campaign said in a post to X, highlighting the debate moment. Bottoms’ sponsorship of the upcoming Halloween event isn’t the first time she has supported drag-themed activities. In 2019, as mayor, she invited Ms. Terra Cotta Sugarbaker, a drag queen, to host a story hour after the Fulton County library system removed a scheduled "drag queen story time" from its events. "Ms. Terra Cotta Sugarbaker and all our LGBTQ friends are always welcome at Atlanta City Hall. How about we host your next story hour? Let’s make it happen!" she wrote in a post to X. RILEY GAINES AND MYKAYLA SKINNER SEND MESSAGE TO SIMONE BILES ON WOMEN'S SPORTS DEBATE AFTER SCOTUS RULING The Bottoms campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the upcoming event, what was included in her sponsorship or whether it was appropriate to have children present for events centered around sexuality and gender expression. articles.title: Trump attacks New York Times over report on 9/11 remembrance plans
articles.summary: President Trump pushed back Friday against a report that he will not attend a ceremony in New York City marking the anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attack after event organizers denied his request to speak at the event. The New York Times reported Friday that the president’s team conveyed Trump’s interest in speaking…
articles.body:
President Trump pushed back Friday against a report that he will not attend a ceremony in New York City marking the anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attack after event organizers denied his request to speak at the event.

The New York Times reported Friday that the president’s team conveyed Trump’s interest in speaking at the event to organizers in recent weeks, citing three unnamed sources with knowledge of the situation.

The National September 11 Memorial and Museum has banned speeches from politicians at the ceremony since 2012.

The president is now expected to attend a memorial service at the Pentagon on this year’s anniversary of the attack, while Vice President Vance will represent the White House at the New York event, the Times reported.

“This is more Corrupt News, I’ve been to New York many times over the years, and no one ever speaks, it’s a ‘solemn ceremony!’” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post responding to the outlet’s reporting.

Trump added that he “would love not to speak, because I’m speaking all the time.”

The president also singled out one of the reporters behind the report, deriding Maggie Haberman as a “Fake Reporter” and “an unattractive person both inside and out” in his Friday post.

“She’s been falsely writing about me for years — She’s a stalker, and should be forced to turn over any and all money that she’s made through her fake reporting on me,” Trump wrote.

Charlie Stadtlander, a spokesperson for the Times’, stood by the outlet’s reporting in a statement shared with The Hill on Friday evening.

“The Times’s reporting is based on information from multiple people with knowledge of the discussions and planning around New York’s Sept. 11 ceremony,” Stadtlander said. “Our journalists sought comment from the White House communications team, who provided a statement that didn’t contradict what we had learned. The president chose to attack the story 24 hours later, singling out one of the four reporters who wrote it. We are confident in the accuracy of the reporting.”

Trump has a history of criticizing the outlet’s coverage of him and his administration.

His Justice Department subpoenaed four Times journalists last month after they reported on potential security risks associated with the president’s new Qatari-gifted Air Force One aircraft. The department later withdrew these subpoenas .

articles.body:
Meta settlement puts pressure on competitors

Meta’s settlement with nearly every state in the country is putting some of its biggest competitors on notice as the Instagram and Facebook parent firm tries to steer an industry standard on kids’ online safety.

After years of scrutiny, the company agreed to pay billions of dollars to states and make significant changes to better protect kids on its platforms, but not without putting the spotlight on competitors TikTok and YouTube to do the same.

In announcing the settlement, Meta published an open letter calling on YouTube and TikTok to “follow their lead,” arguing it is the way for “meaningful progress to happen. Full-page print advertisements on this letter are running in major newspapers throughout the weekend .

While the letter publicly calls out the company, multiple platform changes and monetary awards in the settlement are contingent on other platforms’ responses.

“If you are a target , you want to show that this is a much larger, insidious challenge, and that you are one of many and that you shouldn’t alone be called out,” Eric Schiffer, CEO of Patriarch Organization, a technology and media private equity firm.

“And in the process, you are ensuring that others may contribute financially, as well as influence resolving the matter as a whole,” Schiffer added, calling the move “strategically sound.”

The settlement allows Meta to position itself in the national kids’ online safety fight more favorably after being hammered by parents and lawmakers for years over its platforms’ impact on young users’ physical and mental health.

articles.title: Trump says US has entered deal with Venezuela to take control of 65 billion barrels of oil reserves
articles.summary: President Donald Trump said Friday that his administration has entered a sweeping agreement with Venezuela that, if realized, could give the U.S. access to v...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said Friday that his administration has entered a sweeping agreement with Venezuela that, if realized, could give the U.S. access to vast amounts of the South American country's untapped oil reserves, at cost.

Trump in a social media post announcing the agreement said it was negotiated by Secretary of State Marco Rubio , Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Venezuela's acting President Delcy Rodríguez.

"The United States of America has just entered into an Agreement with the Country of Venezuela on, THE BIGGEST OIL DEAL IN WORLD HISTORY!" Trump wrote.

Rodríguez's government in a statement said the deal involves the development of 17 fields with a proven potential of 65 billion barrels. It said the agreement could draw $100 billion in investment into Venezuela's oil industry and yield over $209 billion in taxes for Caracas.

Rodríguez in a posting on Telegram predicted the deal "will have a significant impact on our nation's revival."

The agreement allows for the United States to partner with an unnamed private operator in Venezuela to create a new private company to take hold of the reserves, according to a U.S. official familiar with the contours of the deal.

The official, who was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity, added that Rodríguez granted the company 100-year rights to develop the oil fields.

The deal gives the United States 55% effective output of the new private company -- including an ownership stake and rights to buy oil at cost. The company would be the second largest corporate holder of proven reserves after Saudi Aramco, according to the official.

Trump is under pressure to show he's lowering oil costs

The announcement comes nearly nine months after the U.S. military at Trump's direction carried out an operation to capture Venezuela's then-President Nicolás Maduro and spirit him to the United States to face federal narcoterrorism and drug trafficking charges.

Trump faces mounting pressure to address high gas prices as the war in Iran on Friday reached a six-month milestone with no conclusion in sight. The U.S. has tapped its strategic petroleum reserves, which in early August fell below 300 million barrels, down by more than 100 million barrels since the start of 2026.

The U.S.-Israel war against Iran has led to a dramatic slowdown of Gulf oil moving through the Strait of Hormuz, which about 20% of the world petroleum passed through prior to the conflict.

The average price of gas in the U.S. stood at about $4.09 a gallon on Friday, according to AAA. The average price was $3.21 at the same time last year.

A significant drop in U.S. gas prices tied to the agreement should not be expected immediately. Experts have repeatedly warned that a substantial boost in Venezuelan oil production will not happen quickly as repairing and expanding infrastructure takes years and requires billions of dollars.

Persuading big American oil companies to return the region could face headwinds given the political uncertainty and decades of badly damaged infrastructure.

Days after the ouster of Maduro, Trump gathered oil executives at the White House and called on them to rush back into Venezuela. Executives expressed interest in the opportunity but there was also a measure of caution given their past experience in the country.

Darren Woods, CEO of ExxonMobil, the largest U.S. oil company, said at that moment he saw the country as "un-investable."

But Trump has insisted that his administration has brought a measure of stability to Venezuela.

He has argued that Venezuela stole U.S. oil when former Venezuelan President Hugo Chávez moved decades ago to nationalize hundreds of foreign-owned assets, including those owned by American oil companies.

Rodríguez, in one of her early moves after taking power, signed a law that opens the nation's oil sector to privatization and reversed a bedrock tenet of the self-proclaimed socialist movement that has ruled the country for more than two decades.

Rubio said on X that the agreement would usher in billions in private investment into Venezuela and lead to lower gas prices in the United States.

"This deal is a huge win for both the American and Venezuelan people," Rubio posted.

The oil bought from the new company would go toward filling the U.S. strategic petroleum reserve and toward military use, according to the U.S. official.

Venezuela has one of the largest oil reserves in the world, with an estimated 303 billion barrels of crude oil in the ground. That's about 17% of the world's supply, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. Unlike other parts of the world, where geologists have to search for untapped oil, the reserves under Venezuela's soil are largely mapped and known, experts say. But because of dilapidated infrastructure, the country only produces about 1% of the world's oil.

Maduro remains jailed in the U.S. He has pleaded not guilty.

articles.title: Kentucky woman indicted on charges she damaged World War II Memorial in Washington
articles.summary: Melissa Farris of Elizabethtown is suspected of spray painting the words “Clean hands dirty $” on the monument and filling a fountain with bubbles.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — A Kentucky woman has been indicted by a federal grand jury on charges that she intentionally damaged The World War II Memorial on the National Mall in Washington, D.C. Melissa Farris is scheduled to be arraigned next week on two felony counts. Grand jurors indicted her Thursday on charges of destroying the veterans’ memorial and destroying government property. An attorney for Farris didn’t immediately respond to an email seeking comment on Friday. Farris, of Elizabethtown, Kentucky, is suspected of spray painting the words “Clean hands dirty $” on the monument and filling a fountain with bubbles on Aug. 13. She was ordered released after her initial court appearance on Aug. 17. President Donald Trump posted about the damage to the memorial on social media with a reference to his repeated claims — without providing evidence — that vandals had been damaging the nearby Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. “Our beautiful World War II Memorial was just hit by Spray Painting Vandals,” Trump wrote his Truth Social site. “First the Reflecting Pool, now this.” A former Olympian was charged in late July with deliberately damaging the Reflecting Pool, but the Justice Department later moved to dismiss that case, saying evidence prosecutors had received refuted the idea that vandals were to blame.

articles.title: Trump eyes Yosemite land swap
articles.summary: {beacon} Energy & Environment Energy & Environment The Big Story Trump eyes Yosemite land swap The Trump administration is eyeing a land swap that would give part of Yosemite National Park to a private company, according to a document submitted to Congress. © George Rose, Getty Images file In the document, obtained by The…
articles.body:
The Trump administration is eyeing a land swap that would give part of Yosemite National Park to a private company, according to a document submitted to Congress.

In the document, obtained by The Hill, the National Park Service (NPS) states that a landowner is seeking to connect their property with a park service road in order to facilitate commercial development.

The agency said it is “working with the landowner on a land exchange that will … enable NPS to convey an interest in land.”

“This will require the landowner to purchase property inside the park or within other NPS units in California,” the document continued.

Separately, responses provided by the Interior Department to a Senate office that were shared with The Hill state that the land swap is a “priority.”

Asked about the proposed land swap, the Interior Department, which oversees NPS, told The Hill that it had not made any final decisions.

“If a proposal advances, the Department will follow established procedures to ensure appropriate coordination, transparency and public involvement consistent with federal law,” it said in a statement.

“There has been no political pressure to reach a predetermined outcome, and claims suggesting the Department is secretly working to hand over National Park Service land to a private developer are false,” the department said.

The proposed land swap was first reported by NOTUS . The news outlet reported that the Trump administration was looking to give the land to a company operated by real-estate developer and investment firm Kingsbarn Realty Capital.

The Hill has attempted to reach Kingsbarn for comment. Lanny Davis told NOTUS that he was an attorney for Kingsbarn and said the company was seeking the land exchange.

“It wasn’t Donald Trump; it was me, liberal Democrat Lanny Davis, former counsel to President Clinton, went to the Department of Interior, and we made the argument that this is a pro-environmental decision to allow this road to be directly built to allow the residents of this privately owned property to gain entrance or exit to the park,” Davis told the news outlet. “The road we’re building is a direct pathway that does not endanger any endangered species, and is simply a road.”

articles.body:
Trump to give speech at Pentagon for 25th anniversary of 9/11

President Trump is set to give a speech at the Pentagon for the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 terror attacks and will not visit Ground Zero.

When asked by a reporter Friday on why he is not going to New York City on Sept. 11, Trump said, “Because I’m going to the Pentagon.”

A White House official told The Hill’s sister network NewsNation that Vice President Vance is “ still traveling to NYC and all three sites will be represented with administration officials in attendance.”

The New York Times reported the president was interested in delivering remarks at the Ground Zero site in Manhattan on the anniversary. Politicians have not been allowed to deliver remarks at the site since 2012.

articles.body:
RFK Jr. seizes on Shapiro’s measles statements

Top Trump administration health officials are seizing on vague information from Pennsylvania to openly question the circumstances of two deaths that state health authorities attributed to measles.

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro (D) on Tuesday stood in front of television cameras and blamed misinformation for declining vaccination rates — specifically calling out the Trump administration and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. His comments touched off a public feud between Shapiro and Kennedy and a flurry of accusations over the scope of the state’s measles outbreak. Earlier this week, Shapiro and Pennsylvania Health Secretary Debra Bogen divulged only minimal information during a press conference about the deaths, citing patient privacy. Shapiro and Bogen said only that the patients were unvaccinated and from Lancaster County. They did not specify ages or whether they were members of the Amish community — or any other religious group that may be more vaccine hesitant. State authorities said the deaths were from “measles-associated” conditions but did not directly say they were caused by measles. The lack of specificity gave Kennedy and other Trump officials room to argue Shapiro was hiding something or lying about their causes of death for political gain. “We don’t know exactly what happened in Pennsylvania yet,” Dr. Mehmet Oz, administrator of the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, said in a Fox Business interview Thursday. “We don’t know if the children died from measles or had another condition that was already attacking them and they happened to get measles at the same time,” Oz said. “Governor Shapiro’s unseemly rush to Lancaster County to convene a national press conference and his giddy delight in announcing two measles deaths was a morose commentary on the contemporary political dialogue,” Kennedy wrote on social platform X.

“The deaths may even have been altogether fabricated by one of the Governor’s hopeful staffers,” the health secretary added. Kennedy has adamantly said he takes no responsibility for the nation’s measles outbreak. He blames the drop in vaccination rates against measles on Biden-era COVID vaccine mandates, rather than his questioning of vaccine safety. Shapiro, meanwhile, blamed Kennedy’s spreading of misinformation for vaccine hesitancy. The back-and-forth between the two over vaccines could be a preview of 2028 messaging . Shapiro is widely expected to run for president, and undoing what Democrats call Kennedy-caused damage to public health will likely be a major issue in his campaign.

articles.title: Canadian broadcaster reverses policy barring use of ‘terrorist attack’ label for 9/11
articles.summary: The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation’s (CBC) walked back its move Friday to advise its journalists not to refer directly to Al Qaeda’s Sept. 11, 2001, attack on the U.S. as an act of terrorism — guidance that garnered widespread criticism from political leaders. In an internal memo this week first reported by The Toronto Sun, CBC’s…
articles.body:
The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation’s (CBC) walked back its move Friday to advise its journalists not to refer directly to Al Qaeda’s Sept. 11, 2001, attack on the U.S. as an act of terrorism — guidance that garnered widespread criticism from political leaders.

In an internal memo this week first reported by The Toronto Sun , CBC’s senior director of journalistic standards and public trust, Basem Boshra, instructed staff to “not refer to the Sept. 11 attacks as terrorist attacks.”

On Wednesday, FBI Director Kash Patel slammed this internal advisory and urged other leaders to do the same.

“Just this year, @FBI has been instrumental in or directly responsible for multiple disruptions of significant terrorist and violent criminal organizations operating within Canada,” Hoekstra said. “Failure to recognize and confront radical and terrorist ideologies significantly endangers our efforts to establish and harmonize a shared national and economic security partnership.”

Pete Hoekstra, the U.S. Ambassador to Canada, similarly decried the CBC’s now-defunct guidance in a social media post Friday morning, hours before the broadcaster removed the policy.

The leader of the Conservative Party of Canada, Pierre Poilievre, also took to social media to urge the CBC to “immediately apologize and retract this directive.”

“To call 9/11 anything other than a terrorist attack is an appalling distortion of history,” Poilievre wrote. “It dishonours the victims and their families, the survivors, and the first responders who suffered from the horrors of that day.”

Following this criticism, which also centered around the decision’s proximity to the 25th anniversary of 9/11, Boshra said in a Friday statement that the outlet would change its policy to not require attribution for labeling the Sept. 11 attack as an act of terrorism.

The CBC director said the paper generally follows guidance to attribute words like “terrorist” and “terrorism” to its sources rather than describing events as such directly.

“After reviewing our current language guidance, we have decided to adjust it to clarify that direct attribution is not required for describing the historic events of 9/11 as terrorism,” Boshra wrote. “We are doing so to remove what has unfortunately (and unintentionally) become an impediment to clarity and public understanding.”

The CBC controversy comes amid heightened tensions this week between the U.S. and its northern neighbor as the countries impose sweeping tariffs on one another in an escalating trade war .

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced the country would match President Trump’s 50 percent tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods “ dollar for dollar .”

The American president hit back this week by threatening additional import taxes and signing an executive order to rename “Lake Ontario” as “Lake America.”

articles.summary: President Donald Trump will appear at the Pentagon to mark the 25th anniversary of the attacks on Sept.
articles.body: President Donald Trump will appear at the Pentagon to mark the 25th anniversary of the attacks on Sept. 11, 2001, instead of visiting Ground Zero in New York City. Asked about why he would not be commemorating the anniversary in his hometown, Trump told reporters Friday, “Because I’m going to the Pentagon.” Vice President JD Vance is instead expected to attend the event in New York City, according to a senior administration official. Other officials will attend a ceremony in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, on the day, the official added. The New York Times first reported that Trump would travel to the Pentagon on 9/11, writing Thursday that the president had initially wanted to go to New York City but decided against it when organizers would not allow him to speak during the Ground Zero program, which traditionally does not permit speeches. The White House has denied that claim, with White House communications director Steven Cheung calling the report “FAKE NEWS” in a post on X Friday. A senior administration official also told reporters Friday that the report was “false” but would not explain further. “As a proud New Yorker, President Trump has spoken about his own experiences watching the horrific events of September 11, 2001,” White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said in a statement. “On the 25th anniversary of this tragic day, the President will remember those who were killed at the hands of evil terrorists, honor their loved ones, and pay tribute to the brave first responders who put their lives on the line to rescue their fellow Americans.” Trump visited the Pentagon on 9/11 last year before traveling to New York City to spend the evening at a New York Yankees game that honored the victims of the attacks. He did attend the ceremony at Ground Zero in 2024, appearing at the event where his presidential opponent, former Vice President Kamala Harris, and then-President Joe Biden were also in attendance. Trump had last gone to the New York City ceremony in 2016, but did visit a fire station and police precinct in the city in 2021. During his first term, Trump spent the anniversaries at the Pentagon in 2017 and 2019 and went to Shanksville, Pennsylvania, in 2018 and 2020.
